briefing.briefing_description:
Welcome to Lindenmarkt. You'll like it here, mostly.

About 1200 discount stores, each running a middle aisle promotion that rotates every week: eighty-odd seasonal articles, from patio heaters to commemorative garden gnomes, gone the moment they sell out and never restocked, on principle. Buyers size those orders in spreadsheets today, and store managers override the suggestions whenever the numbers look wrong to them. Too often, they are right.

You are here to run Shelfcast: it forecasts demand for every article, every store, every night, and turns that into order suggestions for the distribution centres, with the quiet confidence of something that has never once had to explain itself to a store manager at six in the morning.

You will not write any of the code. Your job is the room: six colleagues who do not agree on what to build next, each with a price you will need to find out. Availability, waste, residual stock, and how often the system gets overridden anyway are what you will be judged on.

One thing nobody tells you on day one: the coffee machine on the third floor is the only system in this building that has never once needed a rollback.
